original_question: Let the 1-bramble number of a continuous graph Gamma(G) be defined as the maximum order of a family of subtrees of Gamma(G) that pairwise come within distance 1, where the order is the minimum number of points needed to hit every subtree in the family. For a fixed small integer k>0, is there a tractable algorithm to decide whether the 1-bramble number of Gamma(G) is at most k?
target_in_paper: Section 3.4 (Treewidth), final open problem after Definitions 12 and 13: deciding whether the 1-bramble number of a continuous graph is at most k for a given small integer k > 0.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact open problem from the treewidth section: it uses the 1-bramble number of the continuous graph Γ(G), describes a bramble as a family of subtrees that pairwise get within distance 1, defines the order via a minimum hitting set, and asks the intended recognition/tractability question for a bound k.
missing_details: The paper works with a finite combinatorial graph G and its associated continuous graph Γ(G), obtained by replacing each edge of G with a unit-length continuous interval (Section 2, Definitions 1, 3, and 4).
The relevant distance is the shortest-path metric on the continuous graph Γ(G), not merely distance along a single edge (Section 2, Definition 3).
A subtree in this paper means a connected cycle-free subgraph of Γ(G), so that term should be made explicit for the question to be stand-alone (Section 2, Definition 7).
The pairwise condition should be stated exactly as: for every two subtrees T1 and T2 in the bramble, there exist points p in T1 and q in T2 with d(p,q) <= 1 (Section 3.4, Definition 12).
The order should be stated as the minimum cardinality of a point set X subseteq Γ(G) that intersects every subtree in the bramble (Section 3.4, Definition 12).

The paper's open problem is a recognition problem for whether the 1-bramble number is at most k for a given small integer k > 0; to make 'tractable' precise and paper-faithful, it should be phrased as asking for a polynomial-time algorithm.
Definition 13 identifies the 1-bramble number as the paper's notion of treewidth for a continuous graph, which is implicit in your draft but not stated.
refined_question: Given a finite combinatorial graph G, let Γ(G) be the continuous graph obtained by replacing each edge of G with a unit-length continuous interval and equipping the resulting space with the shortest-path metric. A 1-bramble of Γ(G) is a set of subtrees of Γ(G) such that for every two subtrees T1 and T2 in the set, there exist points p in T1 and q in T2 with d(p,q) <= 1. The order of a 1-bramble is the minimum cardinality of a set X subseteq Γ(G) that intersects every subtree in the bramble, and the 1-bramble number of Γ(G) is the maximum order over all 1-brambles of Γ(G). For a given small integer k > 0, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether the 1-bramble number of Γ(G) is at most k?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, since Definition 13 defines the treewidth of a continuous graph Γ(G) to be its 1-bramble number, for a given small integer k > 0, is there a polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether the treewidth of Γ(G) is at most k?
justification: The draft clearly targets the only explicit algorithmic open problem in Section 3.4. Definition 12 supplies the exact notion of an r-bramble, including the metric pairwise-distance condition and the hitting-set definition of order, while Definition 13 identifies the 1-bramble number with the paper's notion of treewidth for continuous graphs. To make the question fully stand-alone, one must also import the paper's meanings of Γ(G), the shortest-path metric on a continuous graph, and subtree from Section 2. The paper's wording asks whether recognizing the property '1-bramble number at most k' for a given small integer k > 0 is tractable; the sharpest standard algorithmic rendering of that is a polynomial-time recognition problem.
